title: Notes
use_cases: Use when analyzing the historical development and terminological evolution of Young Adult (YA) fiction in the UK and USA
Use when discussing the application of Crenshaw's intersectionality within children’s and YA literary theory
Configure when categorizing different library classification terms like 'teenager fiction' versus 'young adult'
Implement when comparing demographic representation and diversity milestones in award-winning YA literature
Use when identifying regional cultural differences in teenage rights and responsibilities between the UK and USA
content:
1. 1.
In her most recent work, Trites ([2018](#ref-CR116)), drawing upon Crenshaw’s concept of intersectionality
, argues that ‘*all*childhood is*always*already intersectional’ [the italics have been added here] because, going back to her previous point, young people are powerless
compared to adults (p. 31). Although this balance of power may exist, using a term that usually describes marginalised/oppressed people is incredibly problematic. Especially since readers of and protagonists in Children’s and YA literature are typically white (and heterosexual, cisgendered, and able-bodied for the latter) (Pearson[2016](#ref-CR96); CLPE[2018](#ref-CR34); Ramdarshan Bold[2018](#ref-CR99)).
2. 2.
For example, despite the similarities in social and economic cultures, there are differences in adolescence
in the UK and USA (countries that dominate YA), e.g. In the UK, teenagers have more rights and responsibilities (such as being allowed to get married or drink alcohol) at a younger age (Griffin[1993](#ref-CR56)).
3. 3.
Although Edwards states that ‘it was in 1942 that the new field of writing for teenager became established’, the term ‘young adult’ was coined by the American Library Association in 1966 (Edwards[1954](#ref-CR002), p. 88; Cart[2010](#ref-CR24)). In the UK, librarians began to use the term ‘teenager fiction’ in 1948 after they realised the teenager demographic was not interested in children’s books (Smith[2002](#ref-CR003)).
4. 4.
These studies focus on American YA: there has not been a study that details the evolution of UKYA.

12. 12.
Thomas is the only author of colour
on the Carnegie Medal
2018 shortlist. The 2017 list had no author of colour on it, as will be discussed on p. x. Although THUG did not win the Carnegie Medal it did win the Amnesty CILIP Honour 2018.
